# FDG9043

> DO throw usage error exceptions directly from the Async method, to aid in debuggability.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.2.5.5 Exceptions from Async Methods.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG9043
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: draft

Message: Throw '{0}' before the task of '{1}' starts: move the check out of the async method

FDG9043 reports, in an externally visible async method (public or protected, as the body says), a throw of ArgumentException or an exception derived from it, or a call to one of their static ThrowIf methods (such as ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull), in the method's own body rather than in a lambda or local function. Async iterators and overrides are reported too: their body is their own. A throw that comes after an await or an await foreach in the text of the body, which can depend on the result of an asynchronous operation (FDG9044), is not reported; an await using awaits only at disposal, so it counts only after its statement ends, and an await using declaration does not count. The order is the order in the text, not control flow: a throw in the else branch of an if whose other branch awaits is not reported, and neither is a throw inside the operand of an await (await F(x ?? throw ...)). Other usage errors, such as InvalidOperationException for a wrong state, are not seen, since the same types also report execution errors, so coverage is partial. The fix moves the checks into a method without the async keyword that returns the task of an async implementation, as the body shows, without changing the signature; there is no code fix.

## From the book

Usage error exceptions (see section 7.2) are indicative of an error in the calling code. If you throw a usage error exception directly from the called method that conveys a few benefits over the exception being wrapped inside Tasks:

1. The callstack very clearly indicates where the usage violation came from, making it easier to for the caller to diagnose and fix.
2. There’s no chance that the exception will be ignored when the Task is never awaited.
3. The invalid inputs don’t end up spinning up the Task machinery, only to cause it to spin down again.

One effect of this guidance is that usage error exceptions should not be thrown from `public async` or `protected async` methods. Instead, the public (or protected) method should do usage validation and then defer to a non-public async method (or an async local function, or another means of separating “inside” and “outside” the Task).

```csharp
// Wrong: The exception is thrown inside the Task;
// the call stack will be less clear
public async Task SaveAsync(string filename) {
  if (filename == null)
    throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(filename));

  ...
}

// Right: The exception is thrown instead of a Task being returned.
public Task SaveAsync(string filename) {
  if (filename == null)
    throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(filename));

  return SaveAsyncCore(uri);
}

private async Task SaveAsyncCore(string filename){ ... }
```
